title: Introduction to Psychology
summary: A clear introduction to the main approaches, memory and learning, development, social behaviour and research methods, with data skills and ethics.
audience: Secondary and first-year university students, teachers and curious readers

lessons.title: What psychology is and its main approaches

body.p: Psychology is the scientific study of behaviour and mental processes. Behaviour is what people do and say. Mental processes are what goes on inside: thinking, memory, emotion and perception. Psychologists use evidence from observation and experiments, not only opinion or common sense, to explain why people act as they do.

list: Biological: behaviour is influenced by the brain, genes, hormones and body chemistry.
Behaviourist: behaviour is learned through experience, by association and by reward and punishment.
Cognitive: the mind is like an information processor, with attention, memory and thinking shaping behaviour.
Humanistic: people have a drive to grow, and personal choice and meaning matter.
Psychodynamic: early experiences and unconscious motives influence behaviour.
Social and cultural: groups, norms and context shape what people think and do.

body.p: No approach explains everything. Good psychologists combine several. For example, anxiety before an exam can involve body arousal (biological), past experiences with tests (learning), worrying thoughts (cognitive), and pressure from family or school (social).

body.tip: In exams, do not just describe an approach. Link it to the behaviour in the question and say one strength and one limitation.

body.p: Memory is how we take in, store and recall information. A common model has three stores. Sensory memory holds input for a second or two. Short-term memory holds a small amount, often about seven items, for roughly half a minute unless rehearsed. Long-term memory has very large capacity and can last years.

list: Decay: the memory trace fades with time when unused.
Interference: other memories get in the way of recall.
Retrieval failure: the memory is stored, but the right cue is missing.

body.p: In classical conditioning, a neutral signal paired repeatedly with a natural response comes to produce that response, as in feeling nervous at the sound of a school bell before a test. In operant conditioning, behaviour followed by a reward becomes more likely, and behaviour followed by an unpleasant outcome becomes less likely. Observational learning means we also learn by watching others and copying their actions.

steps: Space your revision over several days instead of one night.
Test yourself from memory instead of rereading.
Link new ideas to what you already know.
Sleep after studying, because sleep helps memories settle.

body.p: Developmental psychology studies how people change from birth to old age in body, thinking, emotion and relationships. A long-running debate asks how much comes from nature (genes and biology) and how much from nurture (environment and experience). Almost everyone now accepts that both interact.

list: Piaget described stages of thinking in childhood, from learning through senses and movement to abstract reasoning in adolescence.
Vygotsky stressed the role of language, culture and guided help from more skilled people.
Attachment research suggests that a warm, reliable bond with a carer in early life supports later wellbeing, although children are resilient and people can form secure relationships later.

body.p: Adolescence brings fast brain, body and social change. Peers become more important and identity is explored. Understanding this helps teachers and parents give guidance that respects growing independence while keeping young people safe.

body.tip: Stage theories are useful maps, not fixed timetables. Children vary and cultures differ.

body.p: Social psychology studies how other people affect what we think, feel and do. Conformity is changing behaviour to fit a group. Obedience is following orders from an authority. Famous experiments in the twentieth century showed that many ordinary people conformed to a group answer or obeyed instructions they believed to be harmful. These studies are also debated because of their ethics and method.

list: Wanting to be liked or to avoid standing out.
Believing the group knows more than we do.
Seeing the authority as legitimate and thinking responsibility belongs to them.

body.p: Stereotypes are fixed ideas about groups. Prejudice is a negative attitude and discrimination is unfair treatment. Contact between groups working towards shared goals, equal status and institutional support can reduce prejudice.

The bystander effect describes how people are less likely to help when others are present, because each assumes someone else will act or is unsure what to do. If you are the one who notices, act or call for help directly, naming a specific person.

Psychology depends on well-designed research. A hypothesis is a testable prediction, for example: students who test themselves score higher than students who only reread. In an experiment, the researcher changes the independent variable (the study method) and measures the dependent variable (the test score) while keeping other things the same. Random allocation helps make the groups comparable.

list: Surveys and questionnaires collect views from many people but rely on honest answers.
Observation records natural behaviour but cannot show cause.
Case studies give deep detail about one person or group but may not generalise.
Correlational studies measure whether two things go together, but correlation does not prove cause.

body.p: Take the scores 4, 7, 7, 9, 10, 12, 15. The mean is the total divided by the number of scores: 64 / 7 = 9.14 (2 decimal places). The median is the middle value when sorted, which is 9. The mode is the most common value, 7. The range is the highest minus the lowest, 15 - 4 = 11. The standard deviation shows how spread out scores are around the mean. For the scores 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9 the mean is 5 and the standard deviation is 2.

list: Informed consent, and parental consent for children.
Protection from harm.
Confidentiality of data.
The right to withdraw.
Debriefing after any necessary deception.

lessons.title: Applying psychology: wellbeing, careers and cautions

body.p: Psychology is applied in schools, hospitals, workplaces, sport, courts and technology design. Clinical and counselling psychologists help people with mental health difficulties. Educational psychologists support learning. Occupational psychologists improve workplaces. Researchers study and test new ideas.

list: Regular sleep, movement and meals support mood and concentration.
Talking with a trusted friend, family member or teacher can reduce stress.
Breaking big tasks into small steps makes problems feel manageable.
Persistent low mood, panic, thoughts of harming yourself, or trouble coping are signs to speak to a doctor, counsellor or trusted adult. Do not wait.

body.p: This course gives general education, not diagnosis or treatment. Do not use what you learn to label friends or family. Only a qualified professional can assess mental health. Also be careful with online quizzes and social media claims about psychology, many of which are exaggerated or untrue.

body.tip: To become a psychologist you usually need a degree and further supervised training. The route and the legal title differ by country, so check your national requirements.

options: The study of the brain only
The scientific study of behaviour and mental processes

quiz.q: Which approach explains behaviour mainly through learning from rewards and punishments?
About how long does unrehearsed information typically stay in short-term memory?
Forgetting because other memories get in the way is called:
Which study strategy is best supported by memory research?
options: One long session the night before

quiz.q: The nature versus nurture debate is about:
options: The balance of genes and environment in shaping behaviour
Whether children should go to school
Which country has the best schools

quiz.q: Which statement about stage theories is the most accurate?
options: Every child follows the exact same timetable
They have been proven wrong in every respect
They are useful maps but children and cultures vary

quiz.q: Why are people less likely to help in an emergency when others are present?
options: Each assumes someone else will act or is unsure what to do

quiz.q: In an experiment testing study methods, the test score is the:
For the scores 4, 7, 7, 9, 10, 12, 15 what is the median?
For the same scores, what is the range?
A study finds that ice cream sales and sunburn rise together. What is the best conclusion?
options: They are correlated, but one does not necessarily cause the other

quiz.q: Which is an ethical requirement in research with people?
options: Hiding the true aim from everyone forever
Informed consent and the right to withdraw
